what: Supernus Pharmaceuticals develops and sells medicines for disorders of the brain and nervous system. Its products treat attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, epilepsy and Parkinson’s disease, with Qelbree for ADHD and Gocovri for Parkinson’s dyskinesia among the larger ones.
customers: Psychiatrists, neurologists and paediatricians in the United States, with the cost paid by commercial insurers and government programmes.
money: Qelbree, a non-stimulant ADHD treatment, plus older ADHD products.
Gocovri, Osmolex and the epilepsy products Trokendi XR and Oxtellar XR.
moat: A commercial sales force aimed at psychiatry and neurology is an asset that takes years and a great deal of money to build, and it can carry additional products at little extra cost. Qelbree’s position as a non-stimulant option matters because stimulants are controlled substances with supply constraints and side effects some patients cannot tolerate.
risks: Reported net income of $450.0M against free cash flow of only $31.0M is a very large gap. A profit several times the cash the business actually generated means a one-off accounting item is doing most of the work, and the price/earnings ratio of 13 is correspondingly misleading.
The older epilepsy products face generic competition, and their revenue declines on a known schedule.
Revenue has flattened at about $1.2B, so new products have to replace the declining ones just to stand still.
Debt of $351.0M against $195.0M of cash is manageable but leaves limited room for a large acquisition.
Seven analysts average a $54.14 target against a $28.35 price — a 91% gap that reflects very different views on the pipeline rather than a forecast.
opportunities: Qelbree is growing, and the non-stimulant ADHD market is genuinely underserved because stimulants do not suit every patient.
The shares trade at about 4.3 times sales and 10.8 times EV/EBITDA.
The specialist sales force can carry acquired products with little incremental cost, which is why companies like this buy rather than discover.
Revenue has grown from $791.0M in 2021 to $1.2B, so the newer products have so far more than replaced the declining ones.
watch: Qelbree prescriptions against the decline in the older epilepsy products. That race decides whether revenue grows or shrinks, and it is more informative than any earnings figure here.
view: Start with the number that will mislead anyone who reads quickly: Supernus reports $450 million of net income and generated $31 million of free cash flow. A company does not earn fourteen times more profit than cash in the ordinary course of business. Something one-off is sitting in that earnings line, which means the price/earnings ratio of 13 is not telling you this is a cheap pharmaceutical company. It is telling you the denominator is wrong. Judge this on EV/EBITDA, where it sits at about 10.8, and on the direction of the product revenue.

The business underneath is a familiar and reasonable one: a specialty pharmaceutical company running a race between declining old products and growing new ones. The epilepsy franchise is going generic on a known schedule, which is a predictable headwind. Against it, Qelbree is growing in ADHD, and its non-stimulant mechanism addresses a real gap — stimulants are controlled substances with supply problems and side effects a meaningful share of patients cannot tolerate. So far the new has outgrown the old: revenue went from $791 million to $1.2 billion.

The asset that does not show up anywhere on the balance sheet is the sales force. Reaching psychiatrists and neurologists takes years and a great deal of money, and once built, that organisation can carry additional products at almost no incremental cost. This is why companies of this type grow by acquisition rather than discovery, and why the right question about Supernus is usually about capital allocation rather than chemistry.

What makes the stock hard is the gap between the price and the analysts — $28 against a $54 average from seven of them. That is not a disagreement about this year’s revenue; it is a disagreement about whether Qelbree and the pipeline are worth much at all. My own read is that the commercial platform is worth more than the market is paying and the earnings line is worth considerably less than it appears, and that the honest way to track this is prescriptions written for Qelbree against the generic erosion schedule. Everything else here is noise.
bull: Qelbree keeps taking share of a non-stimulant ADHD market that stimulants cannot serve, outgrowing the known generic decline, and the specialist sales force adds more products cheaply.
bear: The epilepsy generics bite faster than Qelbree grows, the one-off earnings flatter a business whose real cash generation is thin, and revenue starts shrinking.
